justification: Formed a fresh judgement first, then checked the round-1 fixes against the live pages myself; both agree the article now clears the pass bar. node tools/check-article.mjs and node tools/run-code.mjs both pass green in this worktree (words=5087, prose=3082, run=17/17 executed, sources=6, errors=0, warnings=0). I re-fetched all five Microsoft Learn pages this article cites (best-practices-for-exceptions, exception-handling-statements, the using statement page, exception-throwing, exceptions-and-performance) and checked every quoted clause word-for-word: all of them now verbatim-match the page they are cited to. This closes every sourcing defect either round-1 critic found: (1) 'don't raise exceptions in finally clauses' is now cited to best-practices-for-exceptions#dont-raise-exceptions-in-finally-clauses, where that exact heading lives (was mis-cited to Exception Throwing, which says something else); (2) 'the compiler transforms a using statement into a try-finally statement' is now cited to Exception-handling statements, the page that actually contains that sentence (was mis-cited to the using-statement page); (3) the Try-Parse Pattern quote no longer includes the fabricated lead-in 'the following practice is important:' - the remaining quoted clause matches Exceptions and Performance exactly; (4) the reserved-exception-types sentence (AccessViolationException/IndexOutOfRangeException/NullReferenceException/StackOverflowException) is now an accurate, cited quotation instead of an uncited paraphrase; (5) the reverse-of-declaration-order claim about separate `using` locals no longer borrows the using-statement page's quotation marks for a syntactic form (`using (a, b)`) the code example doesn't use - it now states the parenthesized-form quote separately from the nesting explanation that actually covers `using var` locals. I also independently re-ran the article's TryParse-vs-throw benchmark on different hardware from the article's stated machine (200,000 iterations each): 3 ms vs 725 ms, a ~240x gap, which is squarely inside 'several hundred times' and 'orders of magnitude' as the article and its cited design guidelines describe it - the qualitative performance claim is genuinely grounded, not folklore. The two adsense-specific minor findings from round 1 are also handled substantively rather than cosmetically: the throw-ex-vs-new-exception paragraph now correctly states the two differ in object identity, InnerException and Data (round 1 had this backwards), and the first exercise is renamed from the pillar's generic 'Predict it' to 'Trace it: how many frames survive', which both removes the literal label collision with async-await.md/garbage-collection.md and better names what the exercise actually asks (trace frame survival through a mixed throw/throw-ex chain, not just guess console output). I independently fetched two of the top-ranking results for 'c# exception handling best practices' (Stackify's guide and Code Maze's dedicated throw-vs-throw-ex piece): Stackify never shows a stack trace, has no ExceptionDispatchInfo, no filter-timing discussion, no Try-Parse pattern, and no benchmark; Code Maze does show throw-vs-throw-ex traces and covers ExceptionDispatchInfo, but has no exception filters, no custom-exception guidance, and no performance measurement. Nothing in this article traces back to either page - the running examples (OrderService/OrderRepository, ConfigLoader/Parse, the Chain rethrow chain, the self-relaunching ExceptionDispatchInfo repro, Account/InsufficientFundsException, LoggingResource) are all original constructions with no counterpart in the sources checked. I found no new issues on my own pass: no filler intro/outro, no boilerplate headings, absolute-sounding words ('always', 'never', 'every') are all scoped to genuinely deterministic compiler/runtime mechanics rather than to unsupported generalizations, and the exercise/heading structure, while following the site's shape-Q house style consistently with its siblings (which is the assigned shape, not evidence of low-value templating), introduces no new duplicate phrasing against async-await.md, garbage-collection.md or generics.md that I could find. This is genuine, verified original value over the field - a real engineered repro and a real measured number where even Microsoft's own pages just assert the behavior - with a clean sourcing record after this round's fixes, which is why it clears 8.5 comfortably rather than by a hair.
